title: SSH
tagline: Secure remote access to every server you'll ever run.
overview: SSH is how you reach servers, how Git talks to GitHub, and how many deployments move files. This module covers how SSH secures a connection, how key-based authentication actually works, everyday client usage including tunnels, file transfer, and hardening a server's SSH configuration.
objectives: Explain the SSH client/server model and host key verification.
Explain public-key authentication and protect private keys.
Generate keys, install them, and use ~/.ssh/config and tunnels.
Transfer files with scp, sftp and rsync.
Harden sshd and the surrounding firewall.
concepts: Public keys allowed to log in.
notes: One key per device; revoke individually.
Never disable host key checking globally.

build: A hardened server you can deploy to with one rsync command

tasks.title: Local SSH server
steps: Add a `Host lab` entry in ~/.ssh/config for port 2222.

Break authorized_keys permissions and diagnose with `ssh -v`.

tasks.title: GitHub over SSH
tasks.goal: Switch your repos to SSH remotes.
steps: Add your public key in GitHub → Settings → SSH keys.
Change a remote with `git remote set-url origin git@github.com:you/repo.git`.

lessons.title: SSH fundamentals and key pairs
lessons.summary: How SSH gives you an encrypted shell on a remote machine, and how public-key authentication works.
lessons.simple: **SSH** (Secure Shell) lets you log into and run commands on a remote server over an encrypted connection. Instead of passwords, you normally authenticate with a **key pair**: a private key you keep, and a public key you put on the server.
lessons.technical:
Architecture: an **SSH client** (`ssh`) connects to an **SSH server** daemon (`sshd`) on TCP **port 22**. On first connection the server presents its **host key**; the client shows its fingerprint and stores it in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. If it ever changes unexpectedly you get a loud warning — possibly a man-in-the-middle, or just a rebuilt server.

After key exchange, everything (login, commands, output, file transfers) is encrypted.

**Public-key authentication**:
- The **private key** (`~/.ssh/id_ed25519`) never leaves your machine and should have a passphrase. Permissions must be `600`.
- The **public key** (`id_ed25519.pub`) can be shared freely; you add it to the server's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`.
- At login the server sends a challenge; your client signs it with the private key; the server verifies the signature with the public key. The private key is never transmitted.

Why keys beat passwords: they can't be brute-forced realistically, can't be phished by typing them into a fake prompt, and can be revoked individually per device.
lessons.analogy: The public key is a padlock you hand out freely; the private key is the only key that opens it. You give the server your padlock; to prove it's you, you show you can open it — without ever handing over the key.

example.code:
$ ssh deploy@203.0.113.10
The authenticity of host '203.0.113.10' can't be established.
ED25519 key fingerprint is SHA256:Xb9q...Lk2.
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no)? yes
Warning: Permanently added '203.0.113.10' to the list of known hosts.
deploy@web-1:~$ uptime
 10:02:11 up 31 days,  2:14,  1 user,  load average: 0.12, 0.08, 0.05
deploy@web-1:~$ exit
example.explain: First connection: verify the fingerprint (ideally against what your cloud console shows), then it's pinned in known_hosts.

terms: Server's key proving its identity; pinned in known_hosts.
Secret key kept on your machine (600 permissions).
remember: Private key stays private; public key goes on servers.
Authentication signs a challenge; the key isn't sent.
mistakes: Emailing or committing a private key.
Blindly typing 'yes' to a changed host key warning.
Private key with 644 permissions (SSH refuses it).
interview: How does public-key authentication work in SSH?
practice: Can you explain: why the private key never crosses the network?
Can you debug: 'REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED'.

lessons.title: ssh-keygen, authorized_keys and connecting
lessons.summary: Generate keys, install them on a server, and connect conveniently with ~/.ssh/config.
lessons.simple: You create a key pair with `ssh-keygen`, copy the public key to the server's `authorized_keys`, then connect with `ssh user@host`. An SSH config file saves typing.
lessons.technical:
- Generate: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "alice@laptop"` → `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` and `.pub`. Ed25519 is modern and short; use RSA 4096 only for legacy systems. Set a passphrase; use `ssh-agent` so you type it once per session (`ssh-add`).
- Install: `ssh-copy-id deploy@host`, or append the `.pub` line to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on the server. Server-side permissions: `~/.ssh` = 700, `authorized_keys` = 600, owned by the user — otherwise sshd silently ignores the file.
- Connect: `ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 -p 2222 deploy@203.0.113.10`.
- Run one command: `ssh deploy@host 'sudo systemctl restart app'`.
- Debug: `ssh -v` shows which keys are offered and why auth fails.

`~/.ssh/config`:
```text
Host prod
    HostName 203.0.113.10
    User deploy
    Port 2222
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
```
Now `ssh prod` works. GitHub uses the same mechanism: add your public key in GitHub settings, then `ssh -T git@github.com`.

**Port forwarding**: `ssh -L 5433:localhost:5432 prod` makes the server's private Postgres reachable at your `localhost:5433`, through the encrypted tunnel, without exposing it publicly.
lessons.analogy: `authorized_keys` is the guest list at the server's door. `~/.ssh/config` is your contacts app: you save "prod" once instead of dialing the full number, extension and name every time.

example.code:
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "alice@laptop"
Enter passphrase (empty for no passphrase): ********
Your public key has been saved in /home/alice/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
$ ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub deploy@203.0.113.10
$ ssh deploy@203.0.113.10 'ls -ld ~/.ssh ~/.ssh/authorized_keys'
drwx------ 2 deploy deploy 4096 ... /home/deploy/.ssh
-rw------- 1 deploy deploy   98 ... /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys
$ ssh -T git@github.com
Hi alice! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.
example.explain: Generate, install, verify server-side permissions, and test the same key with GitHub.

terms: Installs your public key on a server.
Holds decrypted keys in memory for the session.
Tunnel a remote port to a local one.
mistakes: Wrong permissions on the server's ~/.ssh, so keys are ignored.
Pasting the private key into authorized_keys.
Exposing databases publicly instead of using an SSH tunnel.
interview: Walk through setting up key login for a new server.
practice: Can you use: an SSH config alias plus a tunnel to a remote Postgres?

lessons.title: SCP/SFTP and SSH security basics
lessons.summary: Copy files over SSH and harden an SSH server.
lessons.simple: **scp**, **sftp** and **rsync** move files over the same encrypted SSH connection. Because SSH is the front door of your servers, it needs basic hardening.
lessons.technical:
File transfer:
- `scp file.txt prod:/tmp/` and `scp prod:/var/log/app.log .` — quick copies; `-r` for directories.
- `sftp prod` — interactive session (`ls`, `get`, `put`).
- `rsync -avz --delete ./build/ prod:/var/www/app/` — syncs only differences; best for deployments and backups.

Hardening `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` (then `sudo systemctl reload ssh`, keeping your current session open in case you lock yourself out):
- `PasswordAuthentication no` — keys only.
- `PermitRootLogin no` — log in as a user, escalate with sudo.
- `PubkeyAuthentication yes`; optionally `AllowUsers deploy`.
- Firewall: allow 22 only from known IPs if possible (cloud security groups, `ufw allow from 198.51.100.0/24 to any port 22`).
- `fail2ban` bans IPs after repeated failures. Changing the port reduces log noise but is not real security.
- Keep OpenSSH updated. Use one key per device so a lost laptop means removing one line from authorized_keys.
- Prefer a bastion/jump host (`ssh -J bastion prod`) or a managed access tool for production fleets.
lessons.analogy: Hardening SSH is securing your front door: no hidden spare key under the mat (passwords), no master key for the whole building in circulation (root login), a camera that bans repeat lock-pickers (fail2ban), and a gate that only opens for known visitors (firewall).

example.code:
$ rsync -avz --delete ./dist/ prod:/var/www/app/
sending incremental file list
index.html
js/app.js
sent 14,302 bytes  received 92 bytes

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config (excerpt)
PasswordAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
AllowUsers deploy

$ sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh     # validate config before reloading
example.explain: rsync only sent changed files. `sshd -t` validates the config so a typo doesn't lock you out after reload.

terms: Single hardened entry point to private servers.
remember: rsync for repeat transfers and deploys.
Test config with `sshd -t` and keep a session open while changing it.
mistakes: Disabling passwords before confirming key login works.
Relying on a non-standard port as 'security'.
Sharing one private key across the whole team.
interview: How would you harden SSH on a fresh server?
scp vs rsync: when do you prefer rsync?
practice: Can you use: deploy a static site with rsync?
Can you build: a hardened sshd_config plus firewall rule set?
